Pronunciation · 3000 Core Vocabulary · Daily Expressions · Connected Speech · Natural Communication

Part 1

How American English Works

Pronouncing words one-by-one is not enough. Natural American English is a system: sounds, stress, rhythm, intonation, and connected speech working together.

Core concepts

TermMeaningWhy it matters
PronunciationHow individual sounds and words are producedAccuracy of /r/, TH, vowels, endings
AccentOverall sound pattern of a variety (e.g., General American)GA is the model here — not Hollywood imitation
FluencySmooth flow of speech with appropriate pacingNot the same as speed or native-like accent
IntelligibilityHow easily listeners understand youHighest priority for most learners
RhythmPattern of stressed and unstressed beatsMakes English sound 'English'
StressExtra energy on a syllable or wordChanges meaning and clarity
IntonationPitch movement across phrasesSignals questions, attitude, politeness
Connected speechHow words link and reduce in real speechWhy listening feels hard

Why correct words can still sound unnatural

A2B1B2

If every syllable is equally strong, if function words are fully pronounced, if there is no linking, and if intonation is flat, speech can be accurate but foreign-sounding. Americans listen for stress peaks and compressed weak syllables.

Examples

  • Word-by-word: I · AM · GO · ING · TO · MEET · YOU · TO · MOR · ROW (unnatural)
  • Natural GA: I'm gonna meet you tomorrow / more carefully: I'm going to meet you tomorrow (with reductions on am/to and stress on meet / TOMorrow)

The mastery path

Sound → Word → Stress → Expression → Sentence → Connected Speech → Conversation

  • Sound: consonants, vowels, diphthongs that affect intelligibility
  • Word: clear citation form + American spelling→sound patterns
  • Stress: correct syllable prominence inside words
  • Expression: chunks and collocations, not isolated translations
  • Sentence: content-word stress and focus
  • Connected speech: linking, weak forms, Flap T, reductions
  • Conversation: management phrases, register, repair strategies

Note

This book supports practice you already do (shadowing, listening, speaking, writing). Use it to check what to aim for and why something sounded different.

Part 2

American English Sound System

A practical map of General American sounds — enough phonetics to train your ear and mouth, without turning into an academic textbook.

Phonemes and minimal pairs

A1A2B1

A phoneme is a sound that can change meaning. Minimal pairs prove a contrast matters: ship/sheep, bit/beat, thin/then.

Examples

  • live /lɪv/ vs leave /liv/
  • bad /bæd/ vs bed /bɛd/
  • full /fʊl/ vs fool /ful/
CategoryWhat to notice in GA
ConsonantsInclude /θ ð ɹ ŋ/; Flap T /ɾ/ in many words
VowelsTense/lax pairs; /æ/; often no British /ɒ/; cot–caught varies by region
Diphthongs/aɪ aʊ ɔɪ eɪ oʊ/ — gliding vowels
Voiced vs voicelessVocal fold vibration: /s/ vs /z/, /f/ vs /v/, /θ/ vs /ð/
SyllablesEvery word has ≥1 syllable; stress picks the strong one(s)
IPAUsed here for clarity; GA symbols (e.g., /ɹ/ or /r/ for American R)

Pronunciation

This book uses a practical GA transcription style, e.g. water /ˈwɔɾɚ/ or /ˈwɑɾɚ/ (regional vowel varies; Flap T is the key American feature).

Part 3

Consonants

Systematic consonant reference for General American. Focus on contrasts that affect intelligibility.

/p/ — voiceless bilabial stop

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Lips close; puff of air at start of stressed syllables (aspiration)

When / How

  • Common spellings: p, pp
  • American note: Aspirated in pin; softer after /s/ as in spin

Examples

  • Words: pen, happy, stop
  • Minimal pairs: pat/bat, peach/beach

/b/ — voiced bilabial stop

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Lips close; vocal folds vibrate

When / How

  • Common spellings: b, bb

Examples

  • Words: be, hobby, job
  • Minimal pairs: pat/bat

/t/ — voiceless alveolar stop

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Tongue tip to ridge behind teeth

When / How

  • Common spellings: t, tt, ed (/t/)
  • American note: See Part 4 for Flap T / aspirated T / glottal T

Examples

  • Words: time, better, cat
  • Minimal pairs: tie/die, write/ride

/d/ — voiced alveolar stop

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Same place as /t/, with voice

When / How

  • Common spellings: d, dd, ed (/d/)
  • American note: May also flap in some contexts

Examples

  • Words: day, ready, made
  • Minimal pairs: tie/die

/k/ — voiceless velar stop

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Back of tongue to soft palate

When / How

  • Common spellings: k, c, ck, ch (school)
  • American note: Aspirated in key

Examples

  • Words: cat, back, school
  • Minimal pairs: coat/goat

/g/ — voiced velar stop

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Same place as /k/, with voice

When / How

  • Common spellings: g, gg

Examples

  • Words: go, bigger, bag
  • Minimal pairs: coat/goat

/f/ — voiceless labiodental fricative

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Upper teeth on lower lip; continuous air

When / How

  • Common spellings: f, ph, gh (laugh)

Examples

  • Words: for, phone, laugh
  • Minimal pairs: fan/van, safe/save

/v/ — voiced labiodental fricative

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Same as /f/ with voice

When / How

  • Common spellings: v
  • American note: of usually /əv/; careful speech may reduce further

Examples

  • Words: very, have, of (/əv/)
  • Minimal pairs: fan/van

/θ/ — voiceless dental fricative (TH)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Tongue lightly between/near teeth; air friction — not /s/ or /t/

When / How

  • Common spellings: th
  • American note: Critical American sound — Part 4

Examples

  • Words: think, both, math
  • Minimal pairs: thin/sin, thigh/tie

/ð/ — voiced dental fricative (TH)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Same place as /θ/ with voice

When / How

  • Common spellings: th
  • American note: Function words often use /ð/

Examples

  • Words: the, this, brother
  • Minimal pairs: then/den, they/day

/s/ — voiceless alveolar fricative

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Narrow groove; hissy air

When / How

  • Common spellings: s, ss, c (city), x

Examples

  • Words: see, miss, race
  • Minimal pairs: sip/zip, price/prize

/z/ — voiced alveolar fricative

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Same as /s/ with voice

When / How

  • Common spellings: z, s (as /z/), x
  • American note: Plural/3rd-person -s often /z/ — Part 13

Examples

  • Words: zoo, easy, dogs
  • Minimal pairs: sip/zip

/ʃ/ — voiceless postalveolar fricative (SH)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Lips rounded; tongue farther back than /s/

When / How

  • Common spellings: sh, ti (nation), ci,ssi

Examples

  • Words: she, nation, pressure
  • Minimal pairs: shoe/chew, ship/chip

/ʒ/ — voiced postalveolar fricative

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Same as /ʃ/ with voice

When / How

  • Common spellings: s (measure), ge (beige)
  • American note: Less common; learn in key words

Examples

  • Words: measure, vision, garage (GA often /ʒ/ or /dʒ/)
  • Minimal pairs: confusion/Confucian (advanced)

/tʃ/ — voiceless affricate (CH)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless. Mouth: Stop + fricative: /t/+/ʃ/

When / How

  • Common spellings: ch, tch, tu (nature)

Examples

  • Words: chair, watch, nature
  • Minimal pairs: chip/ship, cheap/jeep

/dʒ/ — voiced affricate (J)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Stop + fricative: /d/+/ʒ/

When / How

  • Common spellings: j, g (giant), dge

Examples

  • Words: job, bridge, graduate
  • Minimal pairs: jeep/cheap

/h/ — voiceless glottal fricative

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiceless (breath). Mouth: Open vocal tract; breathy onset

When / How

  • Common spellings: h, wh (sometimes)
  • American note: Often reduced/deleted in unstressed he/him/her in fast speech

Examples

  • Words: he, ahead, who
  • Minimal pairs: heat/eat

/m/ — bilabial nasal

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Lips closed; air through nose

When / How

  • Common spellings: m, mm, mb (silent b)

Examples

  • Words: me, summer, comb
  • Minimal pairs: map/nap

/n/ — alveolar nasal

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Tongue tip up; air through nose

When / How

  • Common spellings: n, nn, kn (silent k)

Examples

  • Words: no, dinner, know
  • Minimal pairs: map/nap

/ŋ/ — velar nasal (NG)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Back of tongue up like /k/; nasal airflow — no hard /g/ needed in singer

When / How

  • Common spellings: ng, n before /k g/
  • American note: Part 4 — avoid adding /g/ in -ing for most GA speakers

Examples

  • Words: sing, think, bank
  • Minimal pairs: thin/thing, sin/sing

/l/ — alveolar lateral

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Tongue tip up; air around sides

When / How

  • Common spellings: l, ll
  • American note: Clear L vs dark L — Part 4

Examples

  • Words: like, call, people
  • Minimal pairs: light/right, late/rate

/r/ (/ɹ/) — American rhotic approximant

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Tongue bunched/retroflex; no lip trill; tip not tapping

When / How

  • Common spellings: r, rr, wr
  • American note: Rhotic R — Part 4 (core American feature)

Examples

  • Words: red, car, write
  • Minimal pairs: right/light, raw/law

/w/ — labio-velar approximant

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Rounded lips + raised back tongue; glide

When / How

  • Common spellings: w, wh
  • American note: Keep distinct from /v/

Examples

  • Words: we, always, what
  • Minimal pairs: wet/vet, wine/vine

/j/ — palatal approximant (Y)

A1A2B1

Voicing: voiced. Mouth: Tongue near hard palate; glide into vowel

When / How

  • Common spellings: y, i (onion), u (use=/jus/)
  • American note: you/your often reduce in connected speech

Examples

  • Words: yes, you, music
  • Minimal pairs: yet/jet

Part 4

Important American Sounds

Dedicated training targets for General American: R, TH, Flap T, American T variants, L, and NG.

American R (rhotic)

Rhotic R

A2B1B2

General American pronounces /r/ after vowels: car, hard, first, teacher. (Many British accents drop post-vocalic R.)

When / How

  • Initial: red, right, really — tongue bunched; no lip vibration
  • Medial: very, story, sorry
  • Final / r-colored: car /kɑr/, more /mɔr/, bird /bɝd/, teacher /ˈtitʃɚ/
  • R-colored vowels: /ɝ/ (stressed, bird), /ɚ/ (unstressed, teacher)

Examples

  • car, hard, first, nurse, better, computer
  • Mirror practice: hold tongue tense without touching the roof hard

Common mistakes

cah (dropping R) → car /kɑr/
Keep rhotic R in GA

trilled Spanish-like R → American approximant /ɹ/
No tap/trill for standard GA

TH — /θ/ and /ð/

SoundVoicingTypical words
/θ/voicelessthink, thank, both, math, three, birthday
/ð/voicedthe, this, that, these, those, brother, mother, weather

Common mistakes

tink / sink for think → think with tongue at teeth /θ/
Not /t/ or /s/

dis / zat for this → this /ðɪs/
Voiced TH, not /d/ or /z/

Flap T /ɾ/

When T (and sometimes D) becomes a flap

B1B2C1

In GA, /t/ or /d/ between vowels often becomes a quick tap /ɾ/ when the following syllable is unstressed. It can sound like a soft 'd' to learners.

When / How

  • Common: water, better, city, pretty, waiting, meeting, computer (middle t), Saturday
  • After /n/ sometimes nasal flap: twenty ≈ twenny (casual)
  • Does NOT flap when: T starts a stressed syllable (attain, return), or after consonants in many cases (after), or careful citation speech
  • Spelling still t/tt — pronunciation changes

Examples

  • water /ˈwɔɾɚ/ · better /ˈbɛɾɚ/ · city /ˈsɪɾi/ · pretty /ˈprɪɾi/
  • waiting /ˈweɪɾɪŋ/ · writer ≈ rider in many accents (context disambiguates)

American T variants (practical)

VariantWhereExample
Aspirated [tʰ]Start of stressed syllabletime, attack (second t)
Unaspirated [t]After /s/stop, stay, student
Flap [ɾ]Vowel_T_unstressedVbetter, city
Unreleased [t̚]End of words/phrases (common)cat_, that_ (hold, little release)
Glottalized /ʔ/ influenceBefore /n/ or casual button/mountainbutton ≈ bu'n (casual GA)

Note

Train Flap T and final unreleased T for listening first; produce them gradually so you stay intelligible.

Clear L vs dark L

L quality

B1B2

Clear L (lighter) often before vowels: light, leave, hello. Dark L (tongue back raised) often at ends and before consonants: feel, full, milk, people.

Examples

  • light vs feel
  • law vs ball
  • play vs help

NG /ŋ/

/ŋ/

A2B1

Make /ŋ/ with the tongue position of /k/ but nasal airflow. In words like singer, GA usually has no hard /g/. finger does include /g/: /ˈfɪŋɡɚ/.

Examples

  • sing, singing, thing, think (/ŋk/), bank, long

Common mistakes

sin-gin with hard g in singing → singing /ˈsɪŋɪŋ/
No extra /g/ for most -ing forms

replacing /ŋ/ with /n/ → thing ≠ thin
Keep velar place

American Vowels

Practical GA vowel contrasts that change meaning. Regional variation exists (cot–caught); focus on contrasts that stay important for intelligibility.

ContrastExamplesTip

/æ/ vs /ʌ/cat/cut, bat/but, ran/run/ʌ/ more central (strut)
/ɑ/ vs /ɔ/cot/caught (merged for many Americans)If merged, both may sound like /ɑ/; still learn spellings
/ʊ/ vs /u/full/fool, pull/pool/u/ tenser, often with lip rounding
/ʌ/ vs /ɑ/cut/cot, luck/lockCentral vs open back

Part 6

Schwa & Vowel Reduction

Schwa /ə/ is the most common vowel in American English. Unstressed syllables shrink — this is a major reason American speech sounds fast.

What is schwa?

A2B1B2

Schwa /ə/ is a short, neutral, central vowel in unstressed syllables: about, problem, support, banana.

Examples

  • about /əˈbaʊt/
  • problem /ˈprɑbləm/
  • support /səˈpɔrt/
  • photograph /ˈfoʊtəɡræf/ vs photography /fəˈtɑɡrəfi/

Function-word reduction

B1B2C1

Small grammar words often reduce in natural speech: a, an, the, to, for, of, and, can, you…

Examples

  • the → /ðə/ before consonants; /ði/ before vowels (careful)
  • to → /tə/ : want to go ≈ wanna go (casual)
  • for → /fɚ/ or /fər/: for a minute
  • and → /ən/ or /n/: rock and roll ≈ rock 'n' roll
  • can (ability) → /kən/; can't stays stronger /kænt/

Warning

Do not reduce content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) the same way. Over-reducing stressed words hurts clarity — especially at work.

Part 7

Word Stress

English is stress-timed at the word level too: one syllable usually carries primary stress. Wrong stress often hurts intelligibility more than a slightly wrong vowel.

Primary vs secondary stress

A2B1B2

Primary stress is the strongest syllable. Longer words may also have secondary stress.

Examples

  • comPUter · inforMAtion · ˌengiˈneer
  • PHOtograph · phoTOgraphy · photoGRAPHic
PatternExamples
Two-syllable nouns often first syllableTAble, WINdow, PROblem (many exceptions)
Two-syllable verbs often second syllabledeCIDE, beGIN, reCEIVE (many exceptions)
Noun/verb pairsREcord (n) / reCORD (v); OBject / obJECT; PREsent / preSENT
Compounds (nouns)STRES on first: POSToffice, SOFTware, CHECKout
Compounds (adjectives often second when predicative nuance)old-FASHioned; stress can shift with focus
Suffix -tion/-sionStress usually on syllable before: naTION, deCIsion, inforMAtion
Suffix -icStress usually before -ic: ecoNOmic, scienTIfic
Suffix -ityStress before -ity: possiBIlity, creaTIvity
Prefixes un-/re-/in- often unstressedunHAPPy, reWRITE (unless contrastive)

Common mistakes

comPUter with final stress → comPUter /kəmˈpjutɚ/

DEVelopment with wrong peak → deVELopment /dɪˈvɛləpmənt/

Part 8

Sentence Stress

In sentences, Americans stress content words and reduce function words. Moving the focus stress changes meaning.

Usually stressed (content)Usually unstressed (function)
Nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, WH-words, negativesa/an/the, to/of/for, and/but, pronouns, aux (unless focused)

Focus and contrastive stress

B1B2C1

New or important information gets the nuclear stress. Contrastive stress highlights an alternative.

Examples

  • I need the rePORT (not the slides).
  • SHE fixed it (not me).
  • I didn't say he stole the money. (deny saying)
  • I didn't say HE stole the money. (someone else?)
  • I didn't say he STOLE the money. (maybe borrowed)
  • I didn't say he stole the MONEY. (maybe something else)

Part 9

American Rhythm

American English rhythm is stress-timed: stressed syllables come at roughly regular beats, while unstressed syllables compress. That compression — not raw speed — often makes speech sound fast.

Stressed beats and thought groups

B1B2C1

Speak in thought groups (chunks of meaning). Inside each group, hit content-word beats and shrink the rest.

Examples

  • I'm / WORKing on / the PAYment BUG // I'll UPDate you / after LUNCH.
  • Clap only on capitals while saying the line naturally.
  • Rhythm groups ≈ short phrases between brief pauses
  • Reductions and schwa keep timing even
  • Over-pronouncing every word destroys rhythm and can sound robotic
  • In professional settings, keep rhythm natural but avoid extreme casual reductions

Part 10

Intonation

Pitch movement signals sentence type and attitude. Train patterns that matter for clarity and politeness.

PatternCommon useExample
Falling ↘Statements, WH-questions, confident endsIt's ready↘ · Where do you work↘
Rising ↗Yes/No questions, checking, friendlinessAre you free↗ · Ready↗
Fall-rise ↘↗Uncertainty, polite disagreement, implicationI could↘↗ · It's possible↘↗
List intonationRise on items, fall on lastWe need auth↗, tests↗, and docs↘
Surprise / echoHigher rise or wider rangeYou deleted proDUction↗

Note

Sarcasm often uses exaggerated or mismatched intonation with the words — recognize it in listening; use carefully in speech.

Part 11

Connected Speech

Words blend in natural American speech. Train these processes for listening first, then careful production.

ProcessWhat happensExample
C→V linkingFinal consonant links to next vowelpick_up · turn_off · an_apple
V→V linkingGlide /w/ or /j/ may appeargo_away ≈ go_waway · I_agree ≈ I_yagree
C→C transitionsBlend or simplify clustersbest_time · next_week
Weak formsFunction words reducefor /fɚ/ · to /tə/ · and /ən/
AssimilationSound becomes more like neighborten bells ≈ tem bells (casual) · did you ≈ didʒə
ElisionSound dropsfriendship (d may weaken) · camera ≈ camra
ContractionsGrammar words fuseI'm, don't, we've, she's
Flap TSee Part 4get_out ≈ geɾ_out in fast speech sometimes

Examples

  • What do you want? → Whaddya want? (casual) / What do you want? (careful)
  • Did you eat yet? → Didja eat yet? (casual)
  • Could you help me? → Couldja help me? (casual)

Warning

Professional rule: understand heavy reductions; produce moderate linking and weak forms. Extreme reductions can hurt credibility in interviews and client calls.

Part 13

Final -S Rules

Plural nouns, 3rd-person singular verbs, and possessives share three pronunciation endings: /s/, /z/, /ɪz/.

EndingAfterExamples
/s/voiceless sounds (p t k f θ)cats, books, laughs, months (careful), waits
/z/voiced sounds & vowelsdogs, drives, plays, keys, needs
/ɪz/ or /əz/sibilants /s z ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/buses, boxes, watches, judges, wishes, quizzes

Common mistakes

watchs /watʃs/ → watches /ˈwɑtʃɪz/

dropping -s entirely → She works /wɝks/
Keep the ending audible

Part 14

Final -ED Rules

Past tense, past participles, and many adjectives ending in -ed use /t/, /d/, or /ɪd/.

EndingAfterExamples
/t/voiceless (except /t/)watched, liked, missed, fixed, stopped
/d/voiced (except /d/) & vowelsplayed, called, cleaned, used, loved
/ɪd/ or /əd//t/ or /d/wanted, needed, decided, started, downloaded

Note

Adjective note: aged wine vs aged /ˈeɪdʒɪd/ man — a few adjectives keep /ɪd/ unexpectedly (learned/blessed vary). Learn common ones as chunks.

Common mistakes

wantəd with wrong vowel stress → wanted /ˈwɑntɪd/ — extra syllable only after t/d

watchɛd as two heavy syllables → watched /wɑtʃt/ — one syllable

Part 15

Spelling → Pronunciation

English spelling is partly patterned, partly historical. Use reliable patterns; memorize exceptions.

PatternTypical soundReliability
silent e (make, time)previous vowel 'says its name' oftenUseful tendency; many exceptions
ai/ay, ee/ea/eɪ/, /i/ commonlyHigh but not perfect (said, steak)

Part 17

3000 Core American Vocabulary

Approximately 3050 high-value lexical items prioritized by frequency, usefulness, everyday communication, workplace English, and software/professional contexts. This is not a bilingual dictionary dump — learn words with pronunciation, collocations, and register.

How to read vocabulary entries

  • Headword / lemma: the base dictionary form (e.g., decide).
  • Word family: related forms (decision, decisive) — see Part 18.
  • Active vocabulary: words you can use accurately when speaking/writing.
  • Passive vocabulary: words you recognize in listening/reading.
  • Simple words may have shorter entries; high-value verbs/phrases get collocations.
  • Arabic glosses appear where especially useful — English meaning remains primary.

Note

Use this section as a lookup while shadowing and reading. Add new words to your active set by writing one personal example + two collocations.

Part 19

Collocations

Natural American English is collocational. Learn chunks, not isolated translations.

PatternNatural examples
make + nounmake a decision, make progress, make sense, make a mistake, make time
take + nountake responsibility, take a break, take place, take notes, take into account
do + noundo research, do business, do a favor, do well, do harm
have + nounhave a meeting, have trouble, have an impact, have access
strong/weak adj+strong argument, heavy traffic, high priority, deep concern, soft deadline (casual)
adverb + adjhighly likely, deeply concerned, closely related, widely used
verb + prepdepend on, focus on, consist of, result in, deal with

Examples

  • We need to make a decision by Friday.
  • There is heavy traffic on the bridge.
  • It is highly likely that latency will spike.
  • I'm deeply concerned about the outage window.

Common mistakes

do a decision → make a decision

strong rain → heavy rain

big importance → great/major importance · high importance

Part 22

Confusing Words

Pairs that share translation equivalents or similar forms but differ in American usage.

say / tell

say something (to someone); tell someone something

Examples

  • She said hello. / She told me the plan.

speak / talk

speak = languages/formal address; talk = conversation

Examples

  • speak Arabic; talk to a teammate

hear / listen

hear = perceive; listen = pay attention

Examples

  • Did you hear that? / Listen to the call.

see / watch / look

see=perceive; watch=attention over time; look=direct eyes

Examples

  • see a bug; watch a demo; look at logs

bring / take

bring toward here/listener; take away

Examples

  • Bring your laptop. / Take an umbrella.

borrow / lend

borrow=receive temporarily; lend=give temporarily

Examples

  • borrow a charger / lend me a charger

learn / teach

learn=acquire; teach=instruct

Examples

  • learn Go / teach someone Go

remember / remind

remember=have in memory; remind=cause to remember

Examples

  • I remembered. / Remind me.

job / work

job=countable role; work=uncountable activity

Examples

  • a new job / a lot of work

fun / funny

fun=enjoyable; funny=humorous

Examples

  • The hackathon was fun. / a funny joke

advice / advise

advice=noun (uncountable); advise=verb

Examples

  • some advice / I advise waiting

affect / effect

affect=verb; effect=usually noun

Examples

  • affect latency / the effect

especially / specially

especially=above all; specially=for a special purpose

Examples

  • especially useful / specially designed

actual / current

actual=real; current=present-time

Examples

  • the actual root cause / current status

eventually / finally

eventually=after time passed; finally=at the end of a sequence

Examples

  • It eventually failed. / Finally, we shipped.

sensible / sensitive

sensible=reasonable; sensitive=easily affected/confidential

Examples

  • sensible default / sensitive data

historic / historical

historic=important in history; historical=related to the past

Examples

  • historic launch / historical data

economic / economical

economic=economy-related; economical=money-saving

Examples

  • economic impact / economical plan

raise / rise

raise=transitive; rise=intransitive

Examples

  • raise prices / prices rise

lie / lay

lie=recline; lay=put (object)

Examples

  • lie down / lay the cable

principal / principle

principal=main/head; principle=rule

Examples

  • principal engineer / a principle

complement / compliment

complete vs praise

Examples

  • subject complement / nice compliment

ensure / insure / assure

make certain / insurance / reassure a person

Examples

  • ensure backups; insure a car; assure the client

imply / infer

speaker hints / listener concludes

Examples

  • The email implies… / We inferred…

practice / practise

AmE: practice for noun & verb

Examples

  • practice coding (AmE)

maybe / may be

maybe=adv; may be=verb phrase

Examples

  • Maybe later. / It may be ready.

every day / everyday

every day=each day; everyday=ordinary (adj)

Examples

  • every day / everyday tasks

few / a few

few=negative; a few=some

Examples

  • Few tests failed. / A few tests failed.

in time / on time

before too late / punctual

Examples

  • in time to fix it / on time for standup

at the end / in the end

at finishing point / finally

Examples

  • at the end of the call / in the end we rolled back

Daily Expressions

Natural American expressions by situation. Labels show register — do not treat slang as default.

Greetings

Hey, how's it going?

casual

Meaning: Casual hello + how are you

Context: friends, coworkers

Hey, how's it going? — Pretty good.

Alternatives

Hi, how are you? · What's up?

Good to see you.

neutral

Meaning: Friendly greeting when meeting

Context: work/social

Good to see you — thanks for joining.

Alternatives

Nice to see you.

Long time no see.

informal

Meaning: Haven't met in a while

Context: informal reunion

Long time no see! How have you been?

Alternatives

How was your weekend?

neutral

Meaning: Light personal check-in

Context: Monday mornings

Alternatives

Crazy weather, huh?

casual

Meaning: Comment on weather to open talk

Context: casual

Alternatives

Starting conversations

Got a minute?

casual

Meaning: Ask if someone is free briefly

Context: office/Slack

Alternatives

Spoken note

got a → often linked

Quick question for you.

professional

Meaning: Soft opener before asking

Context: work

Quick question for you — who owns billing?

Alternatives

Can I ask you something quickly?

Ending conversations

neutral

Meaning: Polite end to a call/chat

Context: calls

Alternatives

I'll let you get back to it.

Talk soon.

casual

Meaning: Friendly goodbye

Context: email/Slack/call

Sounds good — talk soon.

Alternatives

Asking for help

Could you give me a hand with this?

neutral

Meaning: Ask for help

Context: work

Could you give me a hand with this query?

Alternatives

Can you help me with…? · Mind helping me…?

I'm stuck on…

professional

Meaning: Signal blocker

Context: standup/work

Alternatives

Asking for clarification

What exactly do you mean by…?

professional

Meaning: Ask for precise meaning

Context: meetings

What exactly do you mean by 'soon'?

Alternatives

Could you clarify…? · Do you mean…?

Just to make sure I understand…

professional

Meaning: Confirm interpretation

Context: work

Alternatives

Confirming

That makes sense.

neutral

Meaning: Show understanding/agreement with logic

Context: discussion

Ah, that makes sense.

Alternatives

Got it. · I see.

Sounds good.

casual

Meaning: Agree with a plan

Context: planning

Alternatives

Agreeing

That's a good point.

professional

Meaning: Validate someone's idea

Context: meetings

Alternatives

Fair point. · I agree.

I'm with you on that.

casual

Meaning: Side with someone

Context: discussion

Alternatives

Disagreeing

I'm not sure I agree.

professional

Meaning: Soft disagreement

Context: meetings

Alternatives

I get where you're coming from, but…

neutral

Meaning: Acknowledge then disagree

Context: debate

Alternatives

Giving opinions

Alternatives

casual

Uncertainty

neutral

Natural Conversational Patterns

Reusable frames Americans use constantly. Practice them until they are automatic.

  • I think…
  • I feel like…
  • I guess…
  • I'm not sure…
  • It depends…
  • As far as I know…
  • From my perspective…
  • The thing is…
  • What I mean is…
  • The main issue is…
  • The problem is…
  • That's a good point.
  • That makes sense.
  • I see what you mean.
  • I'm not sure I agree.
  • Let me think.
  • Give me a second.
  • I'll let you know.
  • To be honest…
  • Basically…
  • More specifically…
  • At the end of the day…
  • Long story short…
  • The way I see it…
  • Correct me if I'm wrong, but…
  • If that makes sense.
  • Does that make sense?
  • You know what I mean?
  • Kind of / sort of…
  • Pretty much…
  • Not really.
  • It turns out…
  • It looks like…
  • It seems like…
  • I'm leaning toward…
  • I'd rather…
  • I'd prefer…
  • I'm fine with…
  • I'm open to…
  • Let's assume…
  • For example…
  • In other words…
  • On the other hand…
  • That said…
  • Having said that…
  • Worst case…
  • Best case…
  • I'll keep you posted.
  • Keep me in the loop.
  • No worries.
  • All good.

Examples

  • The thing is, we don't have enough test coverage yet.
  • What I mean is, we should ship a smaller version first.
  • As far as I know, the cert renews automatically.
  • Correct me if I'm wrong, but this endpoint is public.

Conversation Management

How Americans keep conversations moving: openings, interest signals, repair, and closings.

MoveUseful language
StartGot a minute? / Quick question. / Do you have a second?
Show interestOh really? / No way. / How did that go? / What happened next?
Follow-up questionsWhy do you think that? / How so? / What would that look like?
Interrupt politelySorry to interrupt… / Can I jump in?
Disagree politelyI see it differently. / I'm not sure I agree.
Self-correctSorry — what I meant was… / Let me rephrase.
ClarifyDo you mean X or Y? / Just to clarify…
ConfirmSo we're saying…? / If I understand correctly…
Change topicSpeaking of which… / Anyway… / On a related note…
EndI should let you go. / Talk soon. / Thanks — I'll follow up.

Workplace English

Natural American workplace phrases for meetings, status, feedback, and collaboration.

SituationPhrases
Status updateQuick update:… / Here's where we are:… / We're on track / at risk.

DisagreementI have a concern about… / Have we considered…? / The risk is…
FeedbackOne thing that worked well… / One thing to improve… / Appreciate the thoroughness.
ManagersI wanted to flag… / Do you have bandwidth to discuss…? / I'd like your input on…
ClientsThanks for your patience. / We'll follow up in writing. / Just to confirm requirements…
MeetingsLet's take this offline. / Parking lot that for now. / Action item:…
NegotiationWhat's negotiable? / We can do X if we drop Y. / That trade-off works for us.

Part 27

Software Engineering English

Practical language for standups, code review, bugs, architecture, and engineering collaboration.

Daily standups

  • I'm working on…
  • I've finished…
  • I'm blocked by…
  • I ran into an issue with…
  • No blockers.
  • I'll pick up… next.
  • I could use a second pair of eyes on…

Code reviews

  • I'd suggest…
  • Could we…?
  • This could be simplified…
  • Would it make sense to…?
  • Nit: … (small style comment)
  • Blocking vs non-blocking comment…
  • LGTM / Looks good to me.
  • Can you add a test for…?
  • I'm not sure this handles…

Bugs & incidents

  • I reproduced the issue.
  • It seems to be related to…
  • I found the root cause.
  • I'll push a fix.
  • We need a hotfix.
  • Let's roll back.
  • Severity looks like a Sev-2.
  • I'll write a short postmortem.

Requirements

  • Could you clarify…?
  • What exactly do you mean by…?
  • Are we expecting…?
  • Is this a must-have or nice-to-have?
  • What's out of scope?
  • Do we have acceptance criteria?

Architecture

  • From an architectural perspective…
  • This approach would…
  • The trade-off is…
  • This couples X to Y.
  • We might want to isolate…
  • In terms of scalability…
  • Failure mode would be…

Collaboration

  • I'll sync with…
  • Let's pair on this.
  • Can we spike it for an hour?
  • I'll draft an RFC.
  • Putting up a WIP PR.
  • Please hold off on merging.

Part 28

Interview English

Language for technical and behavioral interviews: structure, clarity, and thinking aloud.

GoalPhrases
Introduce yourselfI'm a … based in …. Recently I've been working on…
Describe experienceIn my last role… / One project I'm proud of… / I owned…
Explain decisionsI chose X because… / The trade-off was… / We considered Y but…
Unknown questionsI haven't done that exact thing, but I'd approach it by…
Thinking timeLet me think about that. / I'd start by clarifying…
ClarifyJust to confirm, are we optimizing for X or Y? / Can I ask a clarifying question?
STAR behavioralSituation… Task… Action… Result… / The outcome was…
Ask interviewerWhat does success look like in this role? / What does the team roadmap look like?
CloseThanks — I enjoyed the conversation. / I'm excited about the opportunity.

Examples

  • Let me think about that. I'd approach it by first clarifying the constraints.
  • My reasoning is that consistency matters more than micro-optimizations here.
  • I'm not entirely sure, but I'd consider a queue to absorb spikes.
  • In that situation, I communicated early, proposed options, and owned the follow-up.

Part 29

American vs Textbook English

Textbook English can be correct but stiff. American conversation prefers contractions, phrasal verbs, discourse markers, and ellipsis — without becoming slang by default.

Textbook / formalNatural neutral AmericanCasual
I am going to examine the issue.I'm going to look into the issue.I'll check it out.
Would you like to proceed?Want to go ahead?Ready to go?
I do not know.I don't know.Dunno. / No idea.
Please inform me when it is completed.Let me know when it's done.Ping me when it's done.
I disagree with that proposal.I'm not sure I agree.Yeah, I'm not buying that.
  • correct but formal — fine in academic writing / careful email
  • natural neutral — best default for work
  • casual — friends / informal teammates
  • slang — labeled and limited; not your default professional voice

Part 30

Listening Reference

Why American speech can be hard to catch — and a decoding strategy you can reuse.

  • Weak forms of function words (to/for/and/can)
  • Reductions (gonna/wanna/kinda) in casual speech
  • Linking across word boundaries
  • Flap T making t/d sound alike
  • Schwa in unstressed syllables
  • Sentence stress hiding unstressed material
  • Intonation carrying attitude
  • Contractions and elision

Decoding strategy

  • 1. Identify stressed words (content peaks).
  • 2. Identify reduced words (likely function words).
  • 3. Identify linking (C→V / V→V).
  • 4. Identify contractions (I'm / don't / we've).
  • 5. Identify missing/reduced sounds (Flap T, dropped t/d).
  • 6. Reconstruct the full careful sentence.

Examples

  • Heard: 'Kinda looks like a race.' → Careful: It kind of looks like a race condition.
  • Heard: 'Lemme see whatcha got.' → Careful: Let me see what you have got / what you've got.

Part 31

Shadowing Reference

You already shadow. Use this as a checklist for quality — not as a replacement course.

ModeFocus
With captionsMap sound → spelling; notice reductions in text
No captionsTrain ear for stress/rhythm/linking
Slow repetitionAccuracy of R, TH, vowels, endings
Normal speedRhythm and connected speech
Record & compareFind mismatches in stress/intonation
Stress imitationCopy content-word peaks only
Rhythm imitationCompress unstressed syllables
Intonation imitationCopy pitch shape on the final focus word

Note

Shadow short clips (10–30 seconds). One feature at a time beats everything at once.

Part 32

Speaking Reference

Tools for real-time speaking: thinking time, repair, paraphrase, and keeping talk going.

  • Let me put it another way.
  • What I'm trying to say is…
  • I can't remember the exact word, but…
  • Basically… / More specifically…
  • Sorry, let me restart.
  • In other words…
  • The short version is…
  • How do you say…?
  • It's kind of like…
  • Does that make sense so far?

Fillers (use lightly)

B1B2C1

Natural fillers buy time: um, uh, like, you know, I mean. Overuse hurts clarity — especially in interviews. Prefer meaningful frames: Let me think.

Part 33

Register

Choose language that fits audience and channel. The same idea can be grammatical in several registers.

RegisterWhere it fitsExample
SlangClose friends; rarely at workThat meeting was a dumpster fire.
CasualTeammates / informal chatI'll ping you when it's done.
Conversational / neutralDefault spoken American EnglishI'll let you know when it's done.
ProfessionalWork meetings, Slack with stakeholdersI'll follow up once the fix is deployed.
FormalCareful email, legal, academic tonePlease be advised that the change has been implemented.
AcademicPapers / formal analysisThe results suggest a significant reduction in latency.

Warning

Do not teach or use slang as if it were standard professional English. Label it and keep it optional.

CEFR Progression

Approximate A1→C2 map for this book's domains. CEFR is not defined by vocabulary count alone.

AreaA1–A2B1–B2C1–C2
PronunciationClear consonants/vowels; -s/-ed; basic stressSchwa, sentence stress, Flap T awareness, linkingFlexible intonation, controlled reductions, high intelligibility at speed
VocabularyHigh-frequency daily wordsCollocations, phrasals, workplace corePrecise professional/academic choices; nuance
ExpressionsGreetings, simple requestsOpinion/softening/clarifying framesSubtle disagreement, negotiation, humor control
ConversationShort exchangesMaintain & repair conversationsLead discussions; manage face/politeness
Workplace / SEBasic status phrasesMeetings, reviews, incidentsArchitecture trade-offs; executive-clear updates
InterviewSimple self-introSTAR stories; clarify questionsThink aloud with structure; negotiate uncertainty

  • That's a good question.
  • That's awesome!
  • That's not going to work for me.
  • This is getting out of hand.
  • What exactly do you mean by…?
  • What if we…?
  • When you get a chance…
  • Would you mind…?

Part 38

Master Reference Checklists

Use these checklists periodically to audit pronunciation, vocabulary, and communication readiness.

Pronunciation Checklist

  • Rhotic R in car/first/teacher
  • TH /θ/ and /ð/ distinct from /s t d z/
  • Flap T recognized in water/better/city
  • Schwa in unstressed syllables
  • -s endings /s z ɪz/ audible
  • -ed endings /t d ɪd/ correct syllable count
  • Word stress on key professional terms
  • Sentence stress on content/focus words
  • Basic linking C→V
  • Intonation fits statements vs yes/no questions

Vocabulary Checklist

  • Can use core A1–A2 words without translation delay
  • Know collocations for make/take/do/get/have
  • Can recognize high-value B1–B2 workplace words
  • Active use of key SE terms (deploy, latency, review…)
  • Word families for decide/develop/communicate…
  • Confusing pairs checked (affect/effect, job/work…)

Expression Checklist

  • Open/close conversations naturally
  • Clarify and confirm without freezing
  • Disagree politely
  • Buy thinking time professionally
  • Register control (casual vs professional)

Connected Speech Checklist

  • Hear gonna/wanna without confusion
  • Decode weak forms of to/for/and/can
  • Reconstruct careful English from casual audio
  • Produce moderate linking without mumbling

Workplace English Checklist

  • Status updates: on track / at risk / blocked
  • Ask for clarification of requirements
  • Give actionable feedback
  • Negotiate deadlines and priorities

Interview English Checklist

  • Clear self-intro under 60–90 seconds
  • STAR behavioral answers
  • Think-aloud frames under pressure
  • Clarifying questions before coding/design
  • Trade-off language (because / trade-off / consider)
